title: the breath again — every claim checked
hook: a student asks one question too many about breath, and the teacher answers anyway, with a king and his officers
carry: the breath again — every claim checked

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: the senses quarreled, and breath settled it by getting up to leave, with all of them rising like bees. Did you ask anyone which text says so? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-three.

Some questions go past the lesson plan. In the Prashna Upanishad, the third student asks one. His name is Kausalya, and he doesn't ask what breath is. He asks where it comes from, how it gets into the body, how it splits itself up, and how it leaves. The teacher's first reply, in paraphrase, is a raised eyebrow: you ask more than you should. Then he answers anyway, because the student is sincere. Today: the map the teacher draws, and what that map is and isn't.
screen: `THE QUESTION PAST THE LESSON PLAN.` → `YOU ASK MORE THAN YOU SHOULD.` → `HE ANSWERS ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Pippalada begins at the source. Breath, he says, is born from the self, the way a shadow falls from a person. It isn't the self. It's what the self casts. Then he gives the picture this chapter is remembered for. Breath works like a king who sends officers out to govern villages: you take this one, you take that one. So breath assigns itself. One current, called apana, works low in the body, with elimination and birth. Breath proper, prana, lives in the eye and ear, the mouth and nose. Samana, in the middle, spreads what's eaten evenly, the way a fire is fed. Vyana moves through the body's channels. And udana rises, and at the end, the text says, carries a person on. Now the claim. You'll find the five winds described online as though they were organs, with locations you could point to on a scan. Check that against the chapter. The Prashna never offers a dissection. It offers a king and his officers, a shadow and the one who casts it. Those are pictures, chosen to teach. Ayurveda's classical texts use the same names to talk about movement in the body, and on this path that's read as a way of noticing: the push down, the spreading, the rise. It isn't a diagnosis, and nobody should treat it as one. And one more thing the text quietly models: a hard question is welcome. The teacher grumbles, then gives his best answer to a student who asked too much.
screen: `BREATH FALLS FROM THE SELF LIKE A SHADOW` · `A KING SENDS OFFICERS TO THE VILLAGES` · `A MAP OF MOVEMENT, NOT A SCAN` · `THE HARD QUESTION GETS ANSWERED`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the officers at work. Sit comfortably and let the breath come on its own. For a few breaths, notice anything that feels like settling downward, the weight of the body on the seat. Then notice the spreading: warmth or ease moving out from the middle. Then notice the small lift at the top of each breath in. You're not finding organs. You're just noticing movement, the way the old map invites. If you pray, you can let one breath be a quiet thanks. The bell holds the time.
The breath again. In the Prashna, breath falls from the self like a shadow and sends out officers, like a king. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. Today, ask one question that goes past the lesson plan, the way Kausalya did. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Teachers of yoga and Ayurveda use the names prana, apana, samana, vyana and udana to describe movements of breath in the body, and some treat them as a way of paying attention rather than as anatomy.

original.note: Sanskrit: the rising breath. in the Prashna Upanishad, the current that rises and at the end carries a person on.

trapdoor: what you thought: the five winds are body parts you could find on a scan.
what it means: in the Prashna, they're breath's officers, sent out like a king's men to govern villages.
what a scholar hears: the same five names turn up in Ayurveda's way of describing movement, read as noticing, not as diagnosis.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

sources.ref: Prashna Upanishad 3.1–2 (Kausalya's question; the teacher says he asks too much, then answers)
Prashna Upanishad 3.3 (breath born from the self like a shadow from a person)
Prashna Upanishad 3.4–10 (the king and his officers; apana, prana, samana, vyana, udana)
Charaka Samhita, Chikitsasthana 28 (vata in five forms: prana, udana, samana, vyana, apana)

notes: Prashna 3.1–2: confirm the paraphrase of Pippalada's reply (that Kausalya asks 'too much' or 'transcendental' questions, and that he answers because Kausalya is devoted to Brahman).

Prashna 3.3–10: confirm the shadow image, the king-and-officers image, and the placements (apana low with excretion and generation; prana in eye, ear, mouth, nose; samana in the middle, distributing food evenly; vyana in the channels; udana rising and leading on at death).

The line 'the classical Ayurveda texts later take up the same names' is a general statement with no citation; an Ayurveda Keeper should confirm or cut it. No specific Ayurvedic text is quoted or dated.
